tldr: When running Rigid Body Dynamics (RBD)—the primary computational bottleneck in robot control—on custom hardware (ASICs), this work combines physics-driven sensitivity analysis with a surrogate model to automatically explore optimal per-variable bit-widths (mixed-precision). This cuts circuit area by up to 1.9× and power consumption by up to 1.8× without sacrificing motion accuracy.

It consists of three stages: Stage 1 prunes the search space using physics-driven variable grouping and sensitivity analysis; Stage 2 constructs a fast trajectory error predictor (surrogate model); and Stage 3 uses Bayesian optimization and local search heuristics to discover the bit-width configuration with minimal hardware cost.
overview:
Enabling robots to move quickly and safely in the real world requires high-speed feedback control in the kHz (sub-millisecond) regime. Rigid Body Dynamics (RBD) accounts for up to 90% of this computation time. While implementing RBD on dedicated hardware (ASICs) helps alleviate this workload, deploying such accelerators within the strict battery and board-space budgets of edge robots demands massive reductions in circuit area and power consumption.

Quantization—rounding numerical values—is a natural approach to address this. Unlike deep learning tasks like image recognition, however, RBD sits directly inside a closed-loop control system. Tiny numerical errors manifest as joint torque discrepancies, which accumulate and amplify over time as state errors in subsequent steps, potentially leading to instability or falling. Prior works took the safe route by assigning a uniform bit-width (uniform precision) to all variables. However, this ignores the differing importance of individual variables, wasting hardware resources. On the other hand, moving to mixed-precision, where each variable has an individualized bit-width, triggers a combinatorial explosion exceeding $12^{50}$ candidates. Evaluating accuracy via closed-loop dynamics simulation is also far too slow to search practically.

To solve this, the authors developed APEX-RBD, an automated framework that makes mixed-precision exploration tractable. It shrinks the search space via physics-based variable grouping and sensitivity analysis, and constructs a hierarchical surrogate model that predicts trajectory error in milliseconds using just 100 simulation runs. It then pairs Bayesian optimization with domain-informed local search. Validated across a 7-DOF arm, a quadruped, and a humanoid robot, the framework found designs that maintain motion accuracy comparable to uniform precision while cutting area by up to 1.9× and power by up to 1.8×, all within approximately 10 hours on a single standard PC.
contributions: Proposed the first mixed-precision fixed-point exploration framework for robot dynamics (RBD) accelerators that minimizes area and power under motion accuracy and throughput constraints.
Established a methodology combining physics-based variable grouping and module-level sensitivity analysis to slash the vast search space from over $12^{50}$ down to roughly $7^{13}$.
Realized a surrogate model via hierarchical feature engineering reflecting physical causality, accurately predicting final trajectory tracking error in milliseconds using only 100 simulation samples.

Demonstrated post-layout simulations on a TSMC 28nm process across diverse robotic platforms (manipulator, quadruped, humanoid), achieving up to 1.9× area reduction and 1.8× power savings compared to uniform-precision baselines.

sections.heading: Why control-loop dynamics computations demand mixed-precision
sections.summary: Quantization is effective for accelerating Rigid Body Dynamics (RBD)—the core bottleneck in robotic control—on edge ASICs, but error accumulation within the control loop poses a major challenge. Uniform precision wastes hardware resources, while mixed-precision exploration has been intractable due to a combinatorial search space and heavy simulation costs. This paper presents APEX-RBD, an automated exploration framework designed to solve these issues.
sections.details:
Operating autonomous robots stably requires real-time control loops executing in the millisecond range (kHz regime). Rigid Body Dynamics (RBD) sits at the heart of this control loop. Algorithms like the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA), which computes desired joint torques, are heavy chains of multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations that can consume up to 90% of the controller's total execution time.

Dedicated accelerators are actively being developed to handle these computations on edge platforms. Applying quantization by trimming bit-widths reduces the physical footprint of each arithmetic unit, allowing more processing elements to run in parallel on the same silicon area to boost throughput dramatically. Unlike DNNs for vision, however, quantizing robot control presents unique hurdles. DNNs statistically absorb small numerical errors, but RBD directly dictates physical torques inside a closed-loop controller. Minute rounding errors warp the robot's physical trajectory, and this deviated state feeds back into nonlinear dynamics equations. Errors amplify exponentially over time, in the worst case causing the robot to oscillate or fall.

Prior studies (such as DRACO) adopted uniform precision for FPGAs, assigning an identical bit-width across all variables. Yet for ASICs, where bit-widths can be freely customized, uniform precision is extremely inefficient. Inside RBD computations, variables vary widely: some heavily affect trajectory accuracy while others barely matter; similarly, some variables demand costly hardware arithmetic units while others add negligible overhead. Aggressively trimming bits on insensitive, high-frequency variables while retaining high precision for critical ones dramatically reduces circuit footprint and power consumption without degrading tracking accuracy.

However, implementing mixed precision across 50+ variables with 12 candidate bit-widths yields a search space exceeding $12^{50}$. Moreover, verifying each candidate's safety requires running physical simulations; even with 8-way parallel execution, evaluating just 100 candidates takes 8.5 hours. APEX-RBD overcomes this combinatorial explosion and simulation bottleneck.

sections.heading: RBD accelerator structure and the true optimization goal
sections.summary: RBD algorithms rely on a kinematic tree structure with bidirectional dataflows: a forward pass and a backward pass. Because throughput acts as a strict real-time constraint, the goal of hardware optimization is to minimize area and power while satisfying accuracy and throughput targets.
sections.details:
### RBD Algorithms and Accelerator Architecture
Core RBD algorithms, such as RNEA (Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm) and Minv (inversion of the joint-space inertia matrix), compute along a kinematic tree of robot links and joints. RNEA, in particular, exhibits a bidirectional dataflow: a forward pass propagating velocities and accelerations from the base to the end-effector, and a backward pass aggregating forces and torques from the end-effector back to the base. This structure is highly amenable to pipelining, and dedicated accelerators typically parallelize it using multiple MAC units.

### Optimization Objective: Performance is a Constraint, Area and Power are the Goals
Hardware design constantly navigates performance, power, and area (PPA) trade-offs. In robot control, however, simply pushing throughput and latency as high as possible is not the goal. The control frequency needed to keep the control loop stable (e.g., kHz) acts as a fixed hard constraint. Consequently, the number of parallel MAC units needed to hit this throughput is determined upfront, fixing the high-level hardware architecture. The real target to minimize for battery-powered edge robots is chip area and power consumption by optimizing arithmetic data bit-widths. This work targets fixed-point formats that can be implemented efficiently with integer arithmetic logic.

### Limitations of Prior Work and Motivation
Prior uniform-precision methods selected a shared integer bit-width (dynamic range) and fractional bit-width (precision) across all variables, which made brute-force search or direct simulation feasible. However, this lavish design completely disregards the varying quantization sensitivities of different variables. Unlocking lean, mixed-precision optimization requires a smarter exploration strategy that bypasses the need for exhaustive physical simulations.

sections.heading: How APEX-RBD works: Physics-driven pruning, surrogate prediction, and hybrid search
sections.summary: The framework operates in three stages. First, physics-informed variable grouping and sensitivity analysis compress the search space and fix overflow-free integer bit-widths. Next, a hierarchical surrogate model leverages module-level error predictions to estimate trajectory errors in milliseconds. Finally, Bayesian optimization combined with local search identifies the bit-width configuration that minimizes hardware cost.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Search Space Pruning and Sensitivity Analysis (Stage 1)
The first step is to group the vast array of variables to compress the search space:

- **Initial Grouping**: The 50+ variables in RBD are clustered into 27 groups based on their physical and algorithmic roles (e.g., Coriolis terms, link accelerations, output torques). This alone shrinks the search space from $12^{50}$ to $12^{27}$.
- **Module-Level Sensitivity Analysis**: Next, the framework examines computational errors induced by reducing the fractional bit-width of each group. Instead of running heavy end-to-end trajectory simulations, it uses module-level output errors (e.g., torque errors from RNEA) as proxies. Because variable sensitivities depend on the precision of other variables (error coupling), Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) is used across diverse background settings to construct comprehensive sensitivity curves.
- **Group Merging and Integer Bit-Width Determination**: Groups displaying similar sensitivity curve shapes are merged together. By verifying that merging does not exceed tolerable error margins, the design space is pruned down to roughly 13 groups (a search space of approximately $7^{13}$). Integer bit-widths are finalized by taking the maximum dynamic range observed in simulations plus a safety margin to guarantee overflow avoidance.

### 3.3 Predicting Trajectory Error in Milliseconds via Surrogate Modeling (Stage 2)
Because closed-loop simulation cannot be run at every exploration step, a surrogate machine learning model predicts trajectory errors instead. However, collecting massive training datasets for each new design is impractical. The authors chose Random Forest (RF), an ensemble of decision trees, as a model that trains on very small datasets (100 samples) without overfitting while providing fast inference.

Predicting final trajectory error directly from raw bit-widths is difficult due to strong nonlinearities. The authors introduced hierarchical feature engineering aligned with RBD computational flows:
- **Sub-stage 1**: Lightweight RF models train on individual computational modules (e.g., RNEA, Minv) to predict module-level output errors ($e_{RNEA}$, $e_{Minv}$, etc.).
- **Sub-stage 2**: These predicted module errors serve as prior features, combined with domain-specific features (such as the error ratio $e_{RNEA}/e_{Minv}$ or the bottleneck minimum bit-width across sequential computational chains). The top 20 features ranked by RF feature importance are selected to predict final trajectory tracking error.

### 3.4 Hardware-Aware Hybrid Search (Stage 3)
With a rapid error predictor in place, the framework searches for the fractional bit-width combination that minimizes hardware cost:

- **Analytical Cost Estimator**: It queries pre-synthesized lookup tables (LUTs) of multiplier and adder area/power from standard-cell libraries to instantly calculate the total hardware cost for a given bit-width configuration.
- **Bayesian Optimization (Global Search)**: Globally explores promising configurations to minimize the cost function $\text{Cost}(B) = \text{Area} + \lambda \times \text{Power}$ while keeping surrogate-predicted error under the tolerance threshold $\epsilon_{\text{max}}$, pooling the top 30 candidates.
- **Two-Stage Local Search Heuristics**: Bayesian optimization is effective at locating promising regions but struggles with fine-grained local refinement. Two greedy passes refine the pool: a 'cost-driven' pass prioritizing bit reductions on arithmetic units with the largest area/power footprints (compensating by adding bits to low-impact units if errors spike), and a 'sensitivity-guided' pass trimming bits on low-sensitivity variables while protecting high-sensitivity ones.
- **Final Verification**: Real closed-loop physics simulations are run only on the final pool of 30 candidates to verify that accuracy constraints are met, selecting the lowest-cost candidate as the final design.

captions.F3: Relationship between fractional bit-width and output torque error (sensitivity curves) across variable groups in RNEA. Groups like the Coriolis force term exhibit sharp error increases as bit-width drops, whereas others, like external force terms, show negligible error growth.
captions.F4: Correlation plot between predicted trajectory error from the proposed surrogate model and true trajectory error from end-to-end physics simulations. Despite training on only 100 samples, the model achieves high accuracy and ranking consistency with $R^2 = 0.937$ and a Spearman rank correlation of 0.95.

sections.heading: Empirical results: Substantial savings across arm, quadruped, and humanoid platforms
sections.summary: Evaluated on a 7-DOF arm (iiwa), a 12-DOF quadruped (HyQ), and a 29-DOF humanoid (Atlas) using a TSMC 28nm process, APEX-RBD achieved up to 1.9× area reduction and 1.8× power savings over a uniform-precision (24-bit) baseline while matching tracking accuracy. The entire exploration completed in roughly 10.8 hours on a single PC.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
To verify generality, experiments evaluated three robots with distinct degrees of freedom and motion dynamics: the 7-DOF iiwa industrial arm, the 12-DOF HyQ quadruped, and the 29-DOF Atlas humanoid. Forty application trajectories were generated for each platform—including trajectory tracking, trotting, slope climbing, squatting, and dynamic balance—evaluated inside a simulator using the Pinocchio library and Model Predictive Control (MPC). Hardware evaluation used post-place-and-route figures generated with Synopsys IC Compiler on a TSMC 28nm CMOS process.

### 4.2 Surrogate Model Performance and Ablation
The surrogate model was trained on 100 simulation samples. On an 80-sample test set, it achieved $R^2 = 0.937$ and RMSE = 0.307. Candidate ranking is vital for exploration algorithms, and the model yielded a Spearman rank correlation of 0.95 and a Kendall tau of 0.81. An ablation omitting physics-informed hierarchical feature engineering in favor of raw bit-widths led to discovered designs with 12% larger area and 10% higher power consumption.

### 4.3 Comparison of Search Algorithms
Under the same surrogate model and cost function ($\lambda = 10^4$), APEX-RBD was benchmarked against random search, simulated annealing, grid search, and pure Bayesian Optimization (Pure BO). APEX-RBD secured the lowest hardware cost across every error tolerance threshold. The two local search heuristics proved especially effective at refining Pure BO candidates to escape local minima and strip away remaining hardware waste.

### 4.4 End-to-End Hardware Reductions
APEX-RBD designs were compared against a 24-bit uniform baseline (the state-of-the-art uniform design from DRACO), a 32-bit uniform baseline, and alternative mixed-precision approaches. Throughput constraints (MAC parallelism) and motion accuracy were matched across all tests.
- **Versus Uniform Precision**: Compared to the 24-bit uniform baseline, APEX-RBD reduced area by up to 1.9× (~1.7× on iiwa, ~1.9× on Atlas) and power by up to 1.8×. Compared to conservative 32-bit implementations, it achieved up to 3.1× savings in both area and power.
- **Versus Other Exploration Methods**: Compared to mixed-precision designs found by Pure BO alone, APEX-RBD achieved up to 1.5× smaller area and 1.3× lower power, demonstrating the value of the local search heuristics.

### 4.5 Framework Runtime
The full exploration for the iiwa arm took 10.8 hours on a standard workstation (Intel Core i9, 32GB RAM). Given that DRACO required 8 hours for uniform-precision search, completing mixed-precision exploration over a combinatorial search space in comparable time is notable. Data collection (simulation) for surrogate training accounted for 78.95% of runtime, whereas the search itself ran almost instantly. Using a data-efficient Random Forest avoided the estimated 300 additional samples (+18 hours) that a deep neural network would have required.

captions.F5: Hardware cost (area + weighted power) versus trajectory error tolerance. APEX-RBD (red squares) forms a lower Pareto frontier than Pure BO (green circles) and simulated annealing (orange triangles); arrows highlight significant cost reductions contributed by the local search heuristics.
captions.F6: Post-layout area (left) and power consumption (right) comparisons on a TSMC 28nm process. APEX-RBD cuts area by 1.7–1.9× and power by 1.7–1.8× over the 24-bit uniform baseline, and shows a 1.3–1.5× improvement over Pure BO.
captions.F7: Breakdown of exploration runtime for iiwa (10.8 hours total). Simulation data collection accounts for 78.95% of total time as the primary bottleneck, underscoring why making the surrogate model viable with only 100 samples was critical to overall efficiency.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what lies ahead
sections.summary: APEX-RBD is an automated framework that makes mixed-precision fixed-point exploration for robot dynamics accelerators practical within reasonable search times. By pairing physics-informed search space pruning with an efficient surrogate model, it achieves up to 1.9× area savings and 1.8× power savings without compromising motion accuracy.
sections.details:
This paper presented APEX-RBD, an automated framework addressing the computational intractability of mixed-precision exploration for Rigid Body Dynamics (RBD).

By leveraging physics-driven variable grouping and sensitivity analysis to compress the search space, alongside a hierarchical surrogate model incorporating module-level causal structures, the framework achieves millisecond-level trajectory error predictions from just 100 physical simulations. Coupled with analytical hardware cost estimation, Bayesian optimization, and local search heuristics, it pinpoints hardware configurations that minimize area and power under strict accuracy and throughput constraints.

Across experimental platforms ranging from a 7-DOF arm to a 29-DOF humanoid, the framework achieved up to 1.9× smaller circuit area and 1.8× lower power consumption compared to conventional uniform-precision designs. This provides a practical path toward deploying advanced dynamics-based controllers with high energy efficiency and performance on resource-constrained edge autonomous robots.

takeaways: In robot control quantization, numerical sensitivity does not align with hardware cost; optimizing bit-widths per variable via mixed precision offers substantial advantages over uniform precision.

When evaluating control systems with slow simulations, hierarchical feature engineering—decomposing the system along its physical structure and using intermediate module errors as features—is an effective way to address severe data scarcity (few-shot learning).

Even with modern deep learning methods, lightweight models like well-regularized Random Forests can prove far more practical than DNNs in edge design optimization settings where data collection overhead is high.
limitations: The exploration process depends on target operational workloads; facing unexpected edge-case motions or entirely new task environments poses risks of numerical overflow or degraded accuracy.
The current framework focuses on offline design-time exploration and does not support runtime-adaptive architectures that switch bit-widths dynamically during robot operation.

Evaluations were conducted entirely in simulation (Pinocchio coupled with TSMC 28nm ASIC post-layout simulation) and have not yet been validated with fabricated silicon deployed on physical hardware subject to real-world noise and contact forces.
